chapter 00 · overview

Transformer → LLM → Agent

Layer 1

Transformer — an architecture. (t₁…tₙ) → P(tₙ₊₁)

Adds: content-based routing. Every token can look at every other token and pull in exactly what it needs. That's attention, and it's the whole trick. The other half of each block is an MLP (multi-layer perceptron) — two linear layers applied to each position alone.

Layer 2

LLM — the architecture, trained. Weights + a tokenizer + a context window.

Adds: knowledge and instruction-following. Pretraining compresses the corpus into weights; post-training carves an obedient assistant out of a raw text simulator.

Layer 3

Agent — the LLM in a loop, holding tools, pointed at a goal.

Adds: feedback. Actions produce observations; observations re-enter the context; errors get corrected by the world instead of by luck.

01

The transformer

An architecture for turning a sequence into a prediction. 2017, "Attention Is All You Need".

Three questions, and nothing else belongs in an overview: what is it built out of, how is it trained and used, and where does its knowledge actually come from.

1 · What does a typical transformer look like?

This is what one looks like, with every part named:

Three things in that picture are worth naming, because you'll meet them everywhere:

  • Two towers, and most modern models use only one. The encoder (left) reads a whole input at once; the decoder (right) writes an output one token at a time. Translation needs both. ChatGPT-style models are decoder only — delete the left tower and the cross-attention block, feed the prompt in as the beginning of the text, and that's an LLM.
  • Masked attention in the decoder is what stops a word from peeking at words that come after it. Without it the model could see the answer it's meant to predict.
  • Positional encoding is added at the bottom because attention has no built-in sense of order — on its own it would read a sentence as an unordered bag of words.

2 · How is it trained, and how does it predict?

Training and use are the same machine run two different ways. Start with training — the whole model, learned at once:

But what does "learning" mean concretely? Zoom in on a single output position:

Now do that for every position in the sentence at the same time:

The part worth pausing on is that nobody writes the labels. Ordinary machine learning needs humans to annotate examples, which caps you at however much annotation you can afford. For a language model the correct answer is simply the next word that was already sitting in the text — so any text is training data, and the ceiling becomes how much of the internet you can afford to read.

Prediction is the same machine with the answers taken away. There is no ground-truth row to feed in and nothing to compute a loss against, so the model must eat its own output: it produces one word, glues it onto the end of the input, and runs the identical step again — until it predicts END. This is why a reply arrives word by word, and why the model cannot take a word back: by the next step, that word is part of the question it is answering.

So how does it know when to stop? It doesn't — not in any sense involving knowing. END is simply another entry in the vocabulary. GPT-2 has 50 257 tokens and one of them, id 50256, happens to mean "done"; softmax assigns it a probability exactly like cat or the. The halting is done by ordinary code wrapped around the model:

tok = sample(model(context))
if tok == END:        # ← this line is the stopping.
    break             #    It is not inside the model.
context.append(tok)

A transformer is a function that returns a vector of numbers; it cannot halt anything. It only makes END likely, and something else acts on it.

And that likelihood is trained exactly like everything else. Pretraining concatenates documents into one long stream with an end-of-text token inserted between them, so the model learns "text that looks finished → this token comes next". For a chat assistant, post-training then does the same with turn-end tokens on tens of thousands of answers — which is precisely the figure above, where the fifth and final target is END.

Worth drawing the conclusion: the difference between a base model that rambles forever and an assistant that finishes cleanly is not architectural. It is that one extra training stage. And because stopping is a prediction, it can be wrong — which is why every real system also carries a max_tokens cap and explicit stop sequences rather than trusting the token alone.

3 · Where does the information come from?

The answer is blunt: all of it comes from the training text — there is no other source. The weights are a lossy compression of that corpus, and everything the model can do is a consequence of what it read. That's why it knows nothing that happened after its data was collected, why it's fluent on topics the internet covers heavily and unreliable on ones it barely mentions, and why it can produce a confident sentence with nothing behind it: it is reconstructing from a compressed memory, not looking anything up.

One qualification makes that precise. Information reaches a prediction by exactly two routes, and it helps to keep them apart:

  • The weights — the corpus, compressed, fixed the moment training ends. This is why it knows the capital of France.
  • The context — the text in front of it right now, re-read in full on every single token. This is why it can use a document you paste in that no model ever trained on.

Nothing else feeds a prediction. Almost every practical question about these systems — why a knowledge cutoff exists, why retrieval works, why an agent's whole job turns out to be managing what sits in the window — is a question about which of those two routes you are trying to use.

A useful comparison: is this just a hidden Markov model? The instinct is reasonable — both are autoregressive models of a sequence, both factorize P(x₁…x_T) = ∏ P(xₜ | x₍₁:ₜ₋₁₎), and both emit a distribution over a vocabulary at every step. At the level of the task, they are the same object. But they answer the "where is the information" question in opposite ways:

Hidden Markov modelTransformer
The past is…compressed into a latent state zₜkept verbatim and re-read
AssumptionMarkov — given zₜ, the past is irrelevantnone inside the context window
Memory sizefixed (K states)grows with the sequence
Exact best-sequence decodingyes — Viterbiintractable

That last row is the one worth remembering. The Markov assumption is exactly what buys an HMM exact inference — Viterbi and forward–backward are dynamic programming over that factorization. A transformer discards the assumption in exchange for unrestricted access to the whole context, and loses exact decoding with it. Beam search is Viterbi with the structure that made it exact taken away.

The literature does link them, in three different senses. As a model of the data: Xie et al. assume the pretraining distribution is a mixture of HMMs and prove in-context learning is implicit Bayesian inference over the latent concept (OpenReview), extended empirically by Pre-trained LLMs Learn Hidden Markov Models In-context. As a matter of capability: Transformers Learn Shortcuts to Automata (Liu et al., ICLR 2023) shows a shallow transformer can exactly simulate any finite-state automaton — reaching HMM-like behaviour without recurrence. And as a corrective: On Limitation of Transformer for Learning HMMs finds transformers can be worse than RNNs at actually learning them, which is a result that couldn't exist if the analogy were tight.

So: similar in what they compute, opposite in how they store the past. Worth noting that today's state-space models (S4, Mamba) travel back toward the HMM shape — a fixed-size latent state carried forward — trading away exactly the property this comparison hinges on.

Now go and watch one run. Transformer Explainer runs a real GPT-2 live in your browser — nothing to install. Type your own text and the actual next-token distribution appears; hover any token to light up its attention weights; drag the temperature slider and watch the distribution flatten. It is the three questions above, running.

Type thisWhat you should seeWhich question

The keys to the cabinetcheck whether were beats wasQ3 — grammar, tracked across a distance

anything, then raise the temperaturethe spike spreading into a flat distributionQ2 — the guess is a distribution, not a word

The first one is the cross-entropy slide above with real numbers in it — the model's guessed distribution, minus the ground-truth column.

That describes pretraining — the stage that creates raw capability. What turns that into something that answers your question instead of continuing your sentence is §2.

02

From transformer to LLM

The architecture is a blank engine. Training is what makes it a mind — in four distinct stages that do four different jobs.

People collapse "training" into one word, which hides the most useful distinction in the field: pretraining creates capability; post-training creates behavior. Almost nothing an assistant knows was learned after pretraining. Almost nothing about how it acts was learned during it.

  1. Pretraining — compress the corpus One objective: predict the next token, on ~10–20 trillion tokens of web, code, books, papers. To predict well you must implicitly model syntax, facts, arithmetic, code semantics, and the intentions of whoever wrote the text. Capability falls out as a side effect of compression. Output: a base model — a text simulator that will happily continue a shopping list or a flame war. It is not an assistant and won't answer your question; it'll write three more questions.
  2. Scaling laws — why anyone bet on this Loss falls as a smooth power law in parameters, data and compute. That predictability is what justified nine-figure training runs. Chinchilla corrected the recipe: for a fixed compute budget, train a smaller model on far more data (~20 tokens per parameter). Inference-cost pressure has since pushed everyone even further past that ratio.
  3. SFT — pick a persona out of the simulator Fine-tune on curated (instruction, ideal response) pairs. This doesn't teach facts; it teaches format and role — "when you see a chat template, be the helpful assistant." Cheap, fast, and it's also where the model learns the tool-call syntax it will use as an agent.
  4. RLHF / DPO — optimize what's easier to judge than to write Humans rank pairs of responses; you train a reward model on those rankings and optimize the policy against it (PPO), or skip the reward model and optimize the preference directly (DPO). This is how tone, refusals, honesty and "don't be sycophantic" get installed. It's also where over-optimization shows up as reward hacking.
  5. RL on verifiable rewards — the reasoning/agent unlock When correctness is checkable by a machine — a unit test passes, a proof checks, a math answer matches — you can skip human raters and let the model explore. It discovers long chains of thought, backtracking, and self-checking on its own, and it learns when to call a tool and how to recover when the tool errors. This stage is the single biggest reason agents got usable.
  6. Inference — everything you actually control Weights are frozen when you use it. Your levers are: the context you assemble (system prompt, examples, retrieved docs, tool results), the sampling settings, and the thinking budget. "Prompt engineering" is really choosing what goes into the attention lookup.

The mental model that saves you the most time. A deployed LLM is a frozen function with no memory. It does not learn from your conversation; it re-reads the entire transcript on every single turn. "It remembered what I said" means "someone put it back in the context." Once you internalize this, agent design stops being mysterious and becomes an engineering question: what belongs in the context window on this turn, and what must be dropped?

03

From LLM to agent

An LLM writes text. An agent changes the world, looks at what changed, and decides what to do next.

The definition worth holding: an agent is an LLM running in a loop, where the model chooses the next action and the loop's exit condition. Everything marketed as an agent framework is bookkeeping around that sentence. Contrast it with a workflow, where you hard-code the sequence of LLM calls — workflows are more predictable and you should prefer them whenever the steps are actually known in advance.

The steps, in order

  1. Define tools as typed schemas A tool is a name, a natural-language description, and a JSON Schema for its arguments. All three go into the context as text — so the description is prompt engineering. Vague description → wrong tool chosen. Aim for few, orthogonal, well-named tools; overlapping tools are the #1 cause of flailing.
  2. Run the loop Call the model. If the response contains a tool call, execute it, append the result as a new message, and call again. If it doesn't, you're done. That's it — that is the entire agent. Add a max-iteration cap and a token budget so a confused model can't spin forever.
  3. Let it think before acting (ReAct) Interleaving reasoning with action beats either alone: the model states what it's trying to establish, acts, reads the result, and revises. Modern models do this natively via extended thinking; the pattern is the same — reasoning is what converts an observation into the next action.
  4. Engineer the context, not the prompt Every lap adds tokens. You will hit the window. The real work is deciding what to keep: compact old turns into a summary, retrieve (RAG) instead of preloading, truncate tool output before it enters, and offload to files so the filesystem — not the context — holds state. A 200k window filled with junk performs worse than a 20k window filled well.
  5. Give it memory Two kinds, and conflating them causes bugs. Working memory = the context window, gone at the end of the session. Long-term memory = something durable (files, a notes directory, a vector store) that the agent explicitly writes to and reads from. Long-term memory is not automatic; it's a tool call.
  6. Close the verification loop This is what separates a demo from something useful. Give the agent a signal it can't fake: run the tests, compile it, lint it, diff it, re-read the file it just wrote. An agent with a ground-truth checker converges; an agent grading its own homework drifts confidently into nonsense.
  7. Decompose — subagents and orchestration When a task needs more exploration than one context can hold, spawn subagents with narrow briefs and have them return conclusions, not raw file dumps. The orchestrator keeps the plan; each subagent burns its own context. Use this for genuine parallelism or context isolation — not as decoration.
  8. Guardrails Tool calls are real side effects. Sandbox execution, allowlist commands, require approval for anything destructive or outward-facing, and treat all tool output as untrusted input — a web page or a file can contain text engineered to hijack the loop (prompt injection). This is the security boundary that doesn't exist at layers 1 and 2.

The whole loop, in twenty lines

messages = [{"role": "user", "content": goal}]

for step in range(MAX_STEPS):                  # always bound it
    reply = model(messages, tools=TOOLS, system=SYSTEM)
    messages.append(reply)

    calls = [b for b in reply.content if b.type == "tool_use"]
    if not calls:                              # no action requested → finished
        return reply.text

    results = []
    for c in calls:
        try:
            out = TOOLS[c.name](**c.input)     # the real side effect
        except Exception as e:
            out = f"error: {e}"                # errors go BACK to the model —
        results.append({"type": "tool_result", # recovering is its job, not yours
                        "tool_use_id": c.id,
                        "content": truncate(out)})
    messages.append({"role": "user", "content": results})

    messages = compact_if_needed(messages)     # context is the scarce resource

Read that loop against layer 1. A tool result is appended as ordinary tokens. The model handles it purely through in-context learning — the same attention lookup from section 01, no weights changed. The entire agent paradigm is attention over a context you keep editing.

Workflow or agent?

WorkflowAgent
Control flowYou write itThe model decides it
Use whenSteps are known in advanceSteps depend on what you find
Cost / latencyPredictableUnbounded unless capped
DebuggabilityGoodRead the trajectory and pray
ExampleExtract → classify → route a ticketFind why this test is flaky and fix it

Default to a workflow. Reach for an agent when the search is genuinely open-ended — that's where paying for the loop buys you something.
